title: Minimum Meeting Rooms
summary: Work out how many rooms an office needs to host every booked meeting.

stages.title: Minimum rooms
stages.requirement:
Meetings are `(start, end)` pairs of minutes with `start < end`. A meeting occupies its room
on the half-open interval `[start, end)`: one meeting can start in a room the instant
another ends. Write `min_rooms(meetings)` returning the minimum number of rooms needed to
host all of them. Return 0 for no meetings.

```python
min_rooms([(0, 30), (5, 10), (15, 20)])  # -> 2
min_rooms([(7, 10), (2, 4)])             # -> 1
min_rooms([(1, 5), (5, 10)])             # -> 1   (back to back)
```

Up to 100,000 meetings, in any order.

hiddenTests.name: test_large
test_matches_sweep_brute_force
hiddenTests.code:
def test_matches_sweep_brute_force():
    import random
    rng = random.Random(11)
    meetings = []
    for _ in range(200):
        s = rng.randint(0, 500)
        meetings.append((s, s + rng.randint(1, 60)))
    peak = max(sum(1 for s, e in meetings if s <= t < e) for t in range(600))
    assert min_rooms(meetings) == peak

hints: Process meetings in order of start time. When a meeting starts, which room is the best to reuse?
Keep a min-heap of end times for rooms in use. If the earliest end is `<=` the new start, reuse that room.
Alternative: sort all starts and all ends separately, then sweep with two pointers, counting concurrent meetings.

solution.explanation:
Sort by start and keep a min-heap of the end times of busy rooms. If the room that frees
up earliest is free by the new meeting's start (`<=`, since intervals are half-open),
reuse it with `heapreplace`. Otherwise open a new room. The heap size never shrinks, so
its final size is the peak number of concurrent meetings.
